Quaint

/KWAYNT/ - rhymes with paint · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Quaint means charmingly old-fashioned.

Guests at the inn always photograph the quaint room keys — iron, palm-sized, and hung on numbered hooks behind the desk.

Worked Example

The river crossing at Dole's Landing still runs by hand-cranked ferry: a flat barge, a chain, and a ferryman who takes coins only. Commuters from the new subdivision call it quaint and mean it fondly — they bring visiting relatives out to ride it — though on foggy mornings more than one has wished, quietly, for a bridge.

Quaint is more particular than 'charming' because the charm must come from old-fashionedness itself: the hand crank, the coin box, the chain. And it is warmer than 'dated' — but watch the edge. Aimed at the wrong target, quaint can condescend, patting a whole way of life on the head.

How Quaint Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

charming

charming: delightful and winning, with nothing said about age

old-world

old-world: belonging to an earlier era's manners and look

Antonyms

modern

modern: of the present moment in style and method

sleek

sleek: smooth, polished, and up-to-the-minute

How Strong Is It? — dated → old-fashioned → quaint

dated vs. quaint

dated vs. quaint: Dated is mildly behind the times, with no warmth in it — a dated slideshow — nothing like quaint.

old-fashioned vs. quaint

old-fashioned vs. quaint: Old-fashioned goes further than dated, belonging plainly to an earlier era, but it stops short of quaint, where the old-fashionedness itself becomes the charm.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — quaint

Root — quaint: whole-word borrowing (Old French cointe, 'clever, elegant,' from Latin cognitus, 'known')

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here — quaint came into Middle English whole, from Old French cointe, 'clever, neat, elegant.' Its meaning then wandered for six centuries: skillfully made, then curiously made, then pleasantly strange, and finally charmingly old-fashioned. The Latin ancestor cognitus ('known') survives elsewhere in English, but so worn and re-dressed that no piece of quaint's spelling will show it to you.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Quaint has relatives on paper — the Latin root behind it also produced words like recognize — but centuries of French wear sanded the connection out of its spelling and sound. A root you cannot see or hear in a word is no help for remembering it, so quaint is best learned as it stands.

Strength Check

Word Choice

affectionate / can condescend

Quaint is affectionate — for cobbled lanes, hand-cranked ferries, iron keys — but it looks down as it smiles, so aim it at things, not at people or communities who might resent being scenery. Charming praises without the antique flavor; old-world supplies the flavor without the smile. The opposite of quaint is not ugly; it is sleek.
